781: A is correct because cost allocation tags on AWS resources label each resource with its owning department, giving the CFO the per-department spending accountability that is required. AWS Budgets then lets the company create budgets and attach an alert threshold, so it can receive a notification when spending reaches 60% of the budget. This combination directly satisfies both the accountability and the notification requirements.
782: B is correct because deploying the EC2 instances in private subnets behind an internal ALB keeps the application off the public internet, and setting the ALB security group inbound source to the office network CIDR block restricts access to traffic arriving over the Site-to-Site VPN. NAT gateways in the public subnets, with an attached internet gateway, allow the instances to initiate outbound connections to download security patches without allowing any inbound access from the internet.
783: D is correct because Amazon QLDB is a fully managed ledger database that maintains an immutable, cryptographically verifiable journal of every change to the data, which is exactly what accounting records require. As a serverless AWS managed service, it removes the operational burden of developing and maintaining the underlying ledger infrastructure, making it the most cost-effective fit.
784: C is correct because AWS Glue DataBrew provides managed data preparation jobs that can run at regular intervals and in parallel. AWS Step Functions orchestrates those jobs, including running specific jobs in a defined order later, and its built-in error handling, automatic retries, and state management remove the operational overhead the company wants to eliminate.
785: C is correct because an Amazon SQS FIFO queue provides exactly-once processing and message deduplication, ensuring the application never processes the same payment twice even when Lambda functions run at scale across multiple Availability Zones. FIFO queues also preserve order, which is important for payment processing workloads, whereas standard queues and event-driven S3 or DynamoDB patterns do not guarantee exactly-once delivery.
786: B is correct because AWS Application Discovery Service is the purpose-built tool for collecting usage, inventory, and configuration data from on-premises servers and workloads to support migration planning. Setting the home Region in AWS Migration Hub aggregates that discovery data in one place so the company can plan and track its migration to AWS.
787: A is correct because AWS Control Tower is deployed from the Organizations management account and establishes a governed multi-account landing zone that centrally audits API calls and logins across all existing and new accounts. Enabling AWS Security Hub adds managed, continuously evaluated compliance checks against the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard, and the Control Tower Account Factory provisions new accounts that automatically inherit the governance guardrails, minimizing cost and additional work.
788: C is correct because an AWS Glue crawler catalogs the Parquet files in the S3 bucket into table metadata that Amazon Athena can query, and Athena runs standard SQL directly against the data in S3 in a fully serverless, pay-per-query model. Since the analysis is only occasional, Athena is far more cost-effective than continuously running Aurora, Redshift, or EMR clusters for the same SQL analysis.
789: A is correct because AWS Control Tower proactive controls use CloudFormation hooks to evaluate deployments before resources are created and block noncompliant ones, such as EC2 instances with public IP addresses or IAM resources with inline policies containing wildcard actions. Detective controls would only detect the noncompliant resources after they are already deployed, whereas the requirement is to prevent deployment in the first place.
790: B and E are correct because configuring Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling across multiple Availability Zones in private subnets (B) adds horizontal scaling to meet the increased demand and high availability, since the failure of an instance or an entire AZ does not take the application down. Configuring an Application Load Balancer in a public subnet (E) distributes incoming web traffic across the Auto Scaling instances, delivering scalability and availability with no rewriting of the web application.
791: D is correct because creating an AWS KMS key and enabling the Lambda console encryption helpers encrypts the environment variables at rest using envelope encryption, so the values are not visible in plaintext. The variables are only decrypted at runtime by callers with kms:Decrypt permission on the key, so developers without that access cannot see the plaintext values, while the other options do not address plaintext environment variables.
792: A is correct because an Amazon Cognito user pool is a fully managed authentication service for millions of application users, and Amazon API Gateway REST APIs with a Cognito authorizer validate the user tokens on every request with no custom authentication code to build or maintain. This fully managed combination provides the most operational efficiency for offering a secured RESTful web analytics API.
793: C is correct because an Amazon EventBridge rule can match the KMS DeleteKey API operation from CloudTrail events, and it can trigger an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook that programmatically cancels the scheduled key deletion. The same rule publishes to an SNS topic to email the administrators, and because EventBridge, Systems Manager Automation, and SNS are all managed services, this design has less operational overhead than writing and maintaining custom Lambda logic.
794: B is correct because AWS Lambda is serverless with pay-per-invocation pricing and zero cost while idle, which is ideal for a program used mainly during one week each month. Each report completes in under 10 minutes, which fits within the 15-minute Lambda execution limit, and an EventBridge rule invokes the function exactly when reports are requested, so reports are generated quickly without paying for continuously running EC2 or ECS capacity.
795: B and D are correct because an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system with scratch storage (B) is a high-performance, parallel shared file system purpose-built for HPC workloads, providing the low-latency, high-throughput storage these jobs need. Attaching an Elastic Fabric Adapter to the EC2 instances (D) provides the low-latency, OS-bypass networking that tightly coupled HPC applications require for inter-instance communication, so both together optimize the environment for storage and networking.
796: B is correct because Amazon Rekognition is a fully managed, pre-trained image analysis API that can detect unwanted or inappropriate content in uploaded photos without any machine learning training. A Lambda function exposed through a Lambda function URL gives the web application a simple serverless endpoint to invoke whenever a new photo is uploaded, whereas Rekognition Video analyzes videos rather than photos.
797: B is correct because AWS supports registering multiple MFA devices, up to eight, on the root user account. If one MFA device is lost, the company can still authenticate to the root user with a remaining device, ensuring continuous access to the account without relying on a recovery process or creating additional privileged accounts.
798: B is correct because an Amazon SNS topic supports HTTP endpoint subscriptions, so each partner can be onboarded simply by subscribing its HTTP endpoint to the topic. Publishing the user IDs once to the topic fans the notification out to all partners, and hundreds of new partners can be added rapidly just by subscribing, making SNS the least-effort and most scalable solution.
799: A is correct because Amazon Comprehend is a fully managed natural language processing API that can extract entities such as ingredient names from text without any machine learning expertise or model training. A Lambda function invoked by S3 Event Notifications on PutObject processes each new recipe file automatically and stores the extracted names in DynamoDB, and since the application can tolerate errors and non-food records, this serverless design is the most cost-effective option.
800: B is correct because a VPC peering connection between the primary account VPC and the secondary account VPC allows the Lambda function running in the primary account to reach the EFS mount targets in the secondary account over private IP addressing. Amazon EFS grows automatically as the company adds files, and peering avoids the cost and overhead of copying data or re-architecting, making it the most cost-effective solution.
